4854-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
A secret treaty between Elizabeth and Parma lies at the heart of this 1587 volume, and John Lothrop Motley traces the alarm it spreads through the Dutch States. English commissioners negotiate while Philip, writing at his desk, plots with Parma against England and imagines his general already across the Channel.

Parma himself warns that the scheme is far harder than Philip believes, and Walsingham soon learns of the Spanish plot. Motley follows De Loo's missions, Parma's flattering letters to the queen, and Leicester's growing unpopularity. The volume shows how peace talks could serve as cover for invasion plans, and how quickly trust evaporated once the double game surfaced.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1587d:
Chapter seventeen of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands exposes a secret treaty between Elizabeth and Parma. Excitement and alarm run through the provinces at the news. The Queen affected concealment, Motley writes, but it was in vain. The States knew everything that was passing before Leicester did.

They seized his secretary Junius, jailed him, and took his master's letter from his hands. Leicester's own handwritten letters to his sovereign were read by the men they plotted against. Motley savours the irony of the great favourite out-spied by shopkeepers. The chapter is a study in early modern intelligence, where posts are opened and courts leak. Beneath the comedy runs a grave point: the republic could no longer trust its English governor, and the alliance that saved it was already rotting.
uslaw-usc-t2-s287d: Section 287d of Title 2 gives the House Parliamentarian spending authority for the office. In line with policies and procedures approved by the Speaker, the Parliamentarian may make such expenditures as may be necessary or appropriate for the functioning of the Office. The section sits in Chapter 9C of Title 2, on the Office of Parliamentarian of the House. The hosted Code text is current through Public Law 119-134. One sentence ties an office's purse to its chief's judgment and the Speaker's rules.
uslaw-usc-t2-s907d:
Section 907d of Title 2 of the United States Code sets a special budget process. It sits in the chapter on powers to cut deficits past a set cap. The process starts after a report from the budget office reaches Congress. That report looks ahead to forced cuts under the deficit rules.

Each standing panel of the Senate may then send in its own options. The options go to the Senate Budget Committee by a set date in October. They must deal with the cuts as they touch that panel's own laws. The Budget Committee may then report a measure to the Senate. The measure may back the reach of the planned cuts in whole or part. The rest of the section works through bills and steps in the Senate.
